statement: Over a $10$-year period, the population of a town grew linearly from $12{,}000$ to $15{,}000$. If the population continues to grow linearly at the same rate, by what percent will it increase over the next $10$ years?

choices.misconception: I divided the 3,000-person increase by the starting population of 12,000, which is the percent increase for the first 10 years, not the next 10.
I divided the 3,000-person increase by the population at the end of the next 10 years, 18,000, instead of by the 15,000 at the start of that period.
I found that the population will be 18,000 and divided by 15,000 to get 1.2, then wrote that ratio as 120% instead of a 20% increase.

hints: Linear growth adds the same number of people every $10$ years.
Find the population after the next $10$ years, then write the increase as a percent of the population at the start of that period.
The population goes from $15{,}000$ to $18{,}000$. Divide the $3{,}000$ increase by $15{,}000$.

solutions.reliable: Linear growth adds the same amount in equal time periods: $15000 - 12000 = 3000$ people per $10$ years. Over the next $10$ years the population goes from $15000$ to $18000$. The percent increase is $\frac{3000}{15000} = 0.20$, or $20\%$. Key idea: linear growth adds a constant amount, so its percent increase shrinks as the base grows, and a percent change is always measured from the value at the start of the period.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
